Structural risk surface

Elevation, slope, and paved-surface cover come from actual USGS 3DEP and NLCD raster measurements where available; stream distance, population, and vulnerability are interpolated from the nearest real historical events. Click anywhere for a location-specific breakdown.

Storm scenario

Changes the storm-level inputs (season, tropical origin) applied across the whole surface. Place-level conditions stay fixed to what's really there.

Illustrative simulation: surrounding terrain relief is already a real input to the base model (all three storm buttons use it), but its average linear effect is small — the historical data has only one truly extreme episode (Helene) to learn a relief × intensity interaction from. This scenario adds an extra, hypothesis-driven boost proportional to relief on top of the base model's own (small) learned effect, to represent that interaction. Not fitted from data.

Describe a scenario

Uses a real Claude call to read your description when available in this view; otherwise falls back to a comprehensive local phrase interpreter (18 concept categories, ~450 trigger words/phrases, with intensity words like "extremely" and negation like "not urban" both handled) — fully offline, no API needed. Either way, it reports what it applied and why.

What's driving this estimate

Note on imperviousness: this simplified model shows a negative marginal association between paved surface and predicted risk — and this is backed by the real data, not just the model: the most impervious 10% of historical events had only a 1.1% high-consequence rate, versus 8.3% statewide. Likely reasons include engineered stormwater infrastructure and faster emergency response in developed areas, plus many urban reports being minor nuisance flooding. Nearby flood history is split into two signals for the same reason: more minor flood history nearby lowers predicted risk (resilience/preparedness), while more severe flood history clustered nearby raises it (compounding vulnerability) — confirmed as opposite-signed effects when fit separately. Surrounding terrain relief (5km) is included too, though its average linear effect is small once slope/elevation are already in the model — tested directly, including a relief×tropical interaction term, which came back negligible given the data. Tested honestly: is_tropical_event itself carries essentially zero weight once event_month is included — the model gets its seasonal signal from month alone. Extreme values are capped before scoring so one outlier feature can't dominate the estimate through linear extrapolation.
11-feature simplified linear model (now using an explicit "peak hurricane season" flag alongside month, which improved both accuracy and made storm-scenario comparisons mathematically guaranteed to be consistent — hurricane season always scores at least as risky as typical months, by construction, everywhere). Chosen for full client-side transparency; a compared Random Forest scores higher (PR-AUC ~0.22 vs ~0.20 in repeated cross-validation, both models now include the same feature) and is the model reported as this project's primary result. Not an operational flood warning.
Carolina HighGround — Carolina Data Challenge 2026. Data: NOAA Storm Events, USGS 3DEP & NHD, NCDOT, USGS Annual NLCD, FEMA NRI & CRCI.
